newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK lawyers say Tung civil rights curb open to abuse.
newsitem.headline: HK lawyers say Tung civil rights curb open to abuse.

text.p: leading Hong Kong lawyers on Wednesday slammed future leader Tung Chee-hwa's plans to curb civil liberty laws, describing his amendments as badly drafted and "objectionable as a matter of principle".
The influential Bar Council, representing Hong Kong's top barristers (advocates), condemned proposed new clauses as vague and open to abuse by any repressive authorities.

Their statement of objections, sent to China's anointed future chief executive here, deepened concern by pro-democracy activists and Western countries that Beijing may claw back basic freedoms once Britain pulls out.
Tung is a former shipping magnate chosen to replace Governor Chris Patten when British rule ends at midnight on June 30 and Hong Kong becomes a mainly-autonomous region of China.
He provoked a storm of protest when he put into motion China-inspired plans to tighten key clauses in Hong Kong's laws on public order and freedom of association.

Though Tung later diluted his original proposals he failed to mollify critics at home and abroad, already worried about plans to dissolve the elected legislature and to scrap the British-style first-past-the-post election system.
Campaigners fear the changes will snuff out cherished advances in democracy, introduced late in British rule, that angered Beijing.
Tung has proposed outlawing foreign funding of political parties, restrictions on public-assembly rights and compelling organisers to obtain police permission to demonstrate.
His draft amendments have gone to a China-backed shadow Provisional Legislature set up to replace the elected legislature upon the handover.
The provisional chamber is expected to pave the way for the amendments to pass into law as soon as British rule ends.
The Bar Council's paper submitted to Tung's office objected to clauses which permit police to ban demonstrations on the grounds of "national security".
It said such grounds were unjustified and criticised the definition of national security as vague.
"The scope for abuse is obvious," the submission said arguing it put too much power into the hands of the Commissioner of Police.

"Such prohibition will constitute content-based censorship which is inconsistent with international human rights law on freedom of expression and freedom of peaceful assembly and demonstration," it said.
The submission argued Tung's bid to require an all-embracing registration system for any club or society represented "a wholly-unecessary restriction on freedom of association."
"The right to freedom of association is a fundamental right," the Bar Association argued.
The amendment, as drafted, would make criminals out of many innocent people, the paper said.
"A group of professionals meeting monthly on every first Friday for a luncheon talk when a guest speaker is invited each time to adress the group ... will find themselves a society.
"If they fail to register (as a society) out of ignorance or otherwise, they will face criminal sanctions."
The Bar Council repeated its objection to the Provisional Legislature which it regards as having no basis in law.
China translated its anger over British democratic reforms in Hong Kong by vowing to dissolve the Legislative Council returned under reforms in 1995.
The Provisional Legislature was selected in December to fill a vacuum until new election laws are drafted.
It is expected to function until it gives Hong Kong substitute electoral legislation and reverses the British reforms. Then new elections are due in mid-1998.
The Bar Association's view is shared by the outgoing British administration and its allies in Europe and North America.
Hong Kong's democratic lobby has threatened to challenge the provisional legislature on constitutional grounds, forcing the chamber to conduct its activities over the border in China itself.
